reason: The story of Messier 30 features clear scientific conflict, a 'fountain of youth' hook, and at least 15 claims supported by multiple independent sources.
story: Deep in the cluster Messier 30, stars are cheating death. Discovered in 1764, this 13-billion-year-old globular cluster is effectively a retirement home for ancient stars. But some residents, known as blue stragglers, look impossibly young. Long ago, the cluster’s core collapsed, packing stars into one of the densest regions in the Milky Way. This cosmic traffic jam forced stars into dangerous interactions. Some became 'vampires,' siphoning fresh hydrogen from their neighbors to re-stoke their nuclear fires. Others are 'bad boys' that formed through violent head-on collisions, merging with neighbors to create larger, hotter stars. By stealing mass or crashing together, these stars have effectively reversed their aging process, appearing bluer and brighter than their peers. While the rest of the cluster fades into old age, these stragglers use the chaos of the collapsed core to stay forever young.
angle: Stars in the 13-billion-year-old cluster Messier 30 have found a 'fountain of youth' by siphoning mass from neighbors or physically colliding to reverse their aging process.

claims.claim: Messier 30 was discovered by the astronomer Charles Messier in 1764.
Messier 30 is a globular star cluster.
The cluster is located approximately 27,000 to 28,000 light-years away from Earth.
The cluster is roughly 90 to 93 light-years in diameter.
Messier 30 is approximately 13 billion years old.
The cluster has undergone a process known as core collapse.
Core collapse resulted in a high concentration of mass and star density at the center of the cluster.
The cluster contains 'blue straggler' stars that appear younger and bluer than they should be.
Blue stragglers are more luminous and have higher temperatures than standard stars in the same cluster.
One method of blue straggler formation is mass transfer, where one star siphons material from a companion.
A second method of blue straggler formation is the direct collision and merger of two stars.
Blue stragglers are more heavily concentrated in the central core of the cluster.
Messier originally described the object as a nebula that did not contain stars.
The mass of the cluster is estimated to be between 120,000 and 160,000 times the mass of the Sun.
Core collapse increases the frequency of stellar interactions and collisions.
Blue stragglers stay on the main sequence of star life longer than standard stellar evolution predicts.

disputed: Core collapse timing: Source S3 states the core collapse occurred 1 to 2 billion years ago, but other sources do not provide a date; the script should attribute this timing to a specific study.
Orbit direction: Source S1 claims the cluster has a retrograde orbit, while S4 provides orbital data without explicitly using the term; attribute the orbital flow to specific models.

Interaction frequency: Source S4 suggests close encounters are rare based on X-ray binary counts, while S1 and S3 describe interactions as highly frequent; the script should focus on the 'high density' leading to interactions rather than a specific frequency.
Nicknames: Source S1 identifies the cluster as the 'Jellyfish Cluster,' but this is not mentioned by other sources; omit the nickname to remain conservative.
